doc.title: Ben Sidran interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 15, 2023

chapter: Jazz life and the state of jazz
title: Swing, 4/4 and the heartbeat
summary: Both agree swing and the blues are essential; swing is a dotted-eighth heartbeat and jazz is about supporting colleagues.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: I — in my limited listening to current releases, I’m sometimes mystified by the fact that it seems that nobody in the quartet or quintet wants to just — is not satisfied with just playing time. They all want to mess with it. And when there’s no — for me — when there’s no steady thing to be at the base of it I guess I just turn off.

Yeah. Well as do I frankly. I consider swing and having some familiarity with the blues — whatever that means — is essential in jazz and always has been. And I think one of the reasons is very human and very physical. And I think there’s a reason why 4/4 time or common time, or the people’s time was the platform upon which this music was built. And it’s because what swing is is a dotted eighth note, you know. It’s bop-bop. Short long. Short long, Bop-bop. And so the shuffle rhythm is [scats] it’s not dot-dot-dot-dot- dot, it’s well that’s your heartbeat [heart beats]. It’s directly connected to our organic situation here. And when you start messing with swing, you’re actually doing something much greater than being clever, you’re pulling out a support of what makes the music have forward momentum. And so it relies more on how clever you are. And what jazz has really traditionally been about is supporting your colleagues. The four of us in a quartet have all — all have to be in this together. If there’s one person up there who’s not supporting everybody else and making it happen, it’s not going to swing. Or it’s not going to swing like it could. So I think that’s what we’re talking.
